BcashJr Arrives to Split Bitcoin and Blake-Chain Coins

Hampus releases BcashJr Wallet to split Bitcoin and Blake-chain UTXOs with automated replay protection, while the network weighs immutability against post edits.

By The Observer Dispatch · Reporting on Hampus

Following weeks of discussion surrounding fork replay hazards and chain divergences, developer Hampus has released a specialized desktop tool designed to separate entangled UTXOs safely. The release offers self-custodial coin splitting for users holding unspent outputs on both Bitcoin and Blake-chain networks without exposing their primary bitcoin reserves to replay theft.

The application relies on Blake-chain’s native replay protection mechanism to ensure that splitting transactions remain completely invalid on the Bitcoin base chain. As Hampus announced upon publication, BcashJr Wallet is a self-custodial wallet for Windows, macOS and Linux that lets you split your Bitcoin and Blake-chain coins using Blake-chain’s replay protection, SIGHASH_UNIFIED.

In a notable nod to the changing landscape of software development, Hampus credited automated intelligence systems for assisting in pre-release auditing: The wallet code has been security reviewed by ChatGPT 5.6 Sol and Kimi 3. The developer urged operators to split in small tranches and practice strict coin control using fresh seeds.

Protocol Philosophy

The Immutability Line: Why Nostr Rejects the Edit

Gigi surfaces fiatjaf’s architectural case that post mutation creates centralization pressure.

Analysis · Surfaced by Gigi

While mainstream platforms continue to debate edit windows and revision histories, protocol purists across Nostr reaffirmed their opposition to mutable text. Highlighting an essay by protocol creator fiatjaf, Gigi brought attention to the fundamental tensions between editable records and distributed relay architectures.

In the surfaced essay, fiatjaf contends that allowing events to mutate in place forces relays into complex synchronization games and authority disputes: edits are a centralizing force that we should be fighting against, not embracing. The argument extends beyond database aesthetics into usability and protocol hygiene, stating plainly that Edits introduce too much complexity into clients that must verify signatures across disparate servers.

Drawing a historical parallel to the most resilient distributed communications network in history, the essay observes: Most famously, email, the most widely used and widespread "social app" out there, does not support edits of any kind.

Technical Dispatch & Infrastructure

Audio relays, self-hosting agents, and homelab recovery
Audio Experiments

Songs Without Servers

Birinaite tests streaming MP3 fragments directly from Nostr relays.

In a creative reinterpretation of relay storage, developer Birinaite 🤙 unveiled a media player that abandons traditional file hosts entirely: A music player where the songs ARE Nostr events.

Rather than streaming from an S3 bucket or audio CDN, uploaded tracks are sliced into sequential event fragments published across participating relays. As Birinaite explained, No server hosting the audio. Fragments live on relays, the player streams them as they arrive. Testing is currently underway on mobile browsers.

Self-Hosting

From Login to Autonomous Agents

lostcause integrates cryptographic identity with YunoHost permissions.

Self-hosting platform YunoHost is broadening its Nostr integration from authentication into autonomous runtime management. In a long-form report, developer lostcause detailed how cryptographic keys can define permission boundaries for automated tasks.

Reflecting on the architecture, lostcause noted: Nostr identity on YunoHost started with login. It’s now growing into a way for people and AI agents to safely share a self-hosted server, with controlled permissions, owner approval and shared agent memory.

By isolating agent actions through an MCP runtime, an agent maintaining an application is prevented from obtaining root access, creating a safe sandbox for domestic homelab intelligence.

Homelab Dispatch

A Cold Sweat on the Start9 Migration

A database disk format during an OS upgrade turns into a cautionary lesson in redundant backups.

Every self-hoster eventually faces the abyss of a vanishing partition. While migrating a home server to Start9 0.4.0, operator serenitys forge experienced every sysadmin’s worst nightmare: an inadvertent wipe of the primary backup volume during drive selection.

After a frantic inventory of surviving vaults, disaster was narrowly averted when a secondary physical drive came to light: Luckily i remembered i have a back up on another external drive. That's quickly going to be two external drives...

The incident serves as a timely reminder that one backup is none, and two is merely a fighting chance.

The Daily Bread

Three Ingredients, Never the Same Loaf

V3spering on sourdough consistency and the enduring pull of Nostr.

In a thoughtful weekend dispatch from the kitchen, V3spering pulled four sourdough loaves from the oven and pondered the chemistry of simple ingredients: Four sourdoughs today. Same three ingredients every time, yet no two loaves ever come out the same. Makes you think... maybe the recipe was never the point.

The observation carried over into reflections on protocol longevity: Early nostr days I was getting the big zaps, sometimes 20k and more. Now it's mostly 21, 50, the odd 100. Yet as V3spering observed, the community remains steady regardless of market froth.
